summary:
We developed "Mascu-Skeletal Diagnosis", an integrated digital health-monitoring and clinical decision-support prototype designed for long-duration spaceflight. The platform features an interactive 3D digital twin of the     astronaut's skeletal system, mapping proposed quantitative ultrasound (QUS) and surface electromyography (sEMG) sensor nodes to specific anatomical regions. It processes these physiological inputs into a prototype Bone Health Index and automatically generates region-specific exercise prescriptions. 

The system addresses a critical capability gap identified by NASA: the current lack of a continuous, in-flight bone-density measurement system. Instead of relying solely on pre- and post-mission DXA scans, our platform proposes continuous, non-ionizing monitoring. Most importantly, it closes the loop between measurement and intervention by routing the generated exercise plans to authorized flight surgeons for review and approval via a secure, role-based workflow. 

This integration is vital because microgravity causes rapid bone loss and muscle atrophy that current exercise devices do not completely eliminate. As missions extend to Mars, the inability to evacuate an injured astronaut makes skeletal fragility a severe risk. By connecting real-time physiological monitoring, data interpretation, and physician-supervised countermeasures into one cohesive system, our project aims to protect astronaut health and ensure mission success in deep space.
details:
Mascu-Skeletal Diagnosis is a digital health-monitoring and clinical decision-support platform designed to track and mitigate musculoskeletal deterioration during long-duration spaceflight. In microgravity, the absence of normal mechanical loading causes astronauts to lose 1% to 1.5%and up to 2%of bone mineral density per month in weight-bearing skeletal sites, leading to cumulative mission losses of 6% to 12% over six months and over 30% to 50% on unmitigated Mars transits, alongside rapid muscle atrophy and neuromuscular deconditioning. Because standard dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) scanners are restricted to pre-flight and post-flight assessments due to strict mass, volume, and radiation limits, in-flight tracking remains a critical blind spot. Our platform bridges this gap by pairing an interactive 3D skeletal digital twin with a 30-node physiological sensor architecture distributed across 18 distinct skeletal regions. Eight quantitative ultrasound (QUS) nodes capture acoustic bone parameters—specifically speed of sound (SOS, where healthy adult baselines average 1,540 to 1,550 m/s) and broadband ultrasound attenuation (BUA, where normal bone density exceeds 70 dB/MHz, osteopenia ranges from 55 to 64.9 dB/MHz, and osteoporosis falls below 55 dB/MHz)—while 22 surface electromyography (sEMG) channels record neuromuscular activation and bilateral symmetry ratios. An analytical engine ingests these multi-modal streams, computes a composite Bone Health Index, stratifies structural and muscular decline into severity tiers, and generates targeted exercise prescriptions featuring explicit sets, repetitions, rest intervals, and ratings of perceived exertion (RPE).

By moving tracking from episodic ground scans to continuous, region-specific monitoring, the platform delivers measurable operational benefits for flight crews and mission medical teams. Rather than treating skeletal loss as a uniform whole-body statistic, the 18-region spatial mapping isolates localized vulnerabilities—such as high-risk load-bearing sites in the lumbar spine, femoral neck, and pelvis—and pairs bone acoustic attenuation with real-time muscular load feedback. Clinical literature demonstrates that QUS parameters correlate strongly with fracture risk and DXA-derived BMD, achieving 89% to 92% sensitivity and 85% to 95% specificity in detecting osteoporotic changes without ionizing radiation. Fusing these metrics with 22 channels of sEMG telemetry allows the analytical engine to detect asymmetric muscle unloading—such as bilateral activation deficits exceeding 10% to 15%—before secondary bone resorption compounds. Furthermore, the system enforces strict clinical governance through a role-based authorization workflow: astronauts review their regional metrics and submit algorithmically generated exercise adjustments, while flight surgeons inspect the underlying telemetry and explicitly approve or reject interventions before execution.

The intended impact is to protect crew physical readiness, reduce fracture and soft-tissue injury risks during high-load mission phases like planetary surface operations or Earth re-entry, and establish a scalable framework for autonomous deep-space healthcare. As human missions extend toward the Moon—where partial 0.16g gravity still yields estimated BMD losses near 0.39% per week—and Mars (0.38g, with losses near 0.22% per week), communication latencies of up to 20 minutes each way and the impossibility of emergency medical evacuation demand onboard tools capable of translating raw physiological telemetry into actionable, clinician-verified countermeasures. Beyond spaceflight, this architecture offers direct translational value for terrestrial healthcare, particularly for immobilized ICU patients, elderly populations experiencing age-related osteopenia and sarcopenia, and remote rehabilitation clinics lacking access to bulky radiological imaging systems.

To build the prototype, our team combined modern web visualization, strongly typed analytical logic, and cloud-backed clinical workflows using React, TypeScript, Three.js, Tailwind CSS, Vite, and Node.js for the front-end environment, alongside Firebase Authentication for role-based account separation and Cloud Firestore for real-time persistence of telemetry states, regional calculations, and medical approval logs. What makes the project distinctive is its fusion of spatial anatomy, multi-modal biomechanics, and human-in-the-loop clinical safety within a single unified interface. Instead of presenting astronauts and flight surgeons with dense, disconnected tables of raw acoustic waveforms and microvolt EMG traces, the Three.js digital twin maps computational indices directly onto an inspectable 3D skeleton, making regional asymmetries and progressive bone-muscle interactions immediately intuitive. Framing the software as a clinical decision-support system rather than an autonomous diagnostic black box also resolves a critical barrier in aerospace medicine: preserving physician authority and auditability while automating routine multi-sensor synthesis and workout parameterization.

Throughout development, our team weighed several physiological, statistical, and engineering factors. Anatomically, we distributed the 8 QUS and 22 sEMG nodes across 18 regions to maximize coverage of load-bearing bones and major muscle pairs while minimizing sensor placement burden on the crew. Analytically, we structured the composite Bone Health Index, Z-score deviation thresholds, and bilateral sEMG symmetry ratios as a transparent, extensible computational framework while maintaining scientific rigor—explicitly recognizing that in vivo QUS measurements carry inherent precision coefficients of variation (roughly 0.4% for SOS and 3.2% to 5.5% for BUA) and require controlled ground-based bed-rest and microgravity clinical validation before serving as standalone diagnostic replacements for DXA. Finally, on the software architecture side, we prioritized low-latency 3D rendering, deterministic parameter traceability from raw sensor inputs to prescribed RPE and load volumes, and clean separation between astronaut telemetry dashboards and physician review queues.
